title: Prefetch controller and fusion hints for paged-KV + FlashAttention
content:
Goal
---
Sketch a lightweight "Prefetch Controller" that coordinates asynchronous page loads for paged-KV and emits fusion/hint metadata to attention kernels (FlashAttention variants). Reduce tail latency from page faults and enable more aggressive kernel fusion without increasing PCIe stalls. This is a working/brainstorm doc — rough experiments included.

Key constraints and motivation
- Many production workloads (long contexts, sparse retrieval, multi-session chat) lead to large KV that doesn’t fit full device memory. Paged-KV avoids OOM by spilling pages to host/NVMe and pulling on demand.
- FlashAttention and fused ops perform best when the runtime can assume steady input availability and predictable memory access. Unexpected page loads block GPU kernels and ruin occupancy.
- We need a controller that reduces in-kernel page faults by moving decision logic to host, prefetching proactively, and providing kernels with fusion-friendly guarantees (or fast failover paths).

High-level design
- Prefetch Controller (host-side daemon within runtime):
  - Maintains soft-usage windows per-session/partition (LRU-ish but with temporal hints).
  - Tracks in-flight prefetches and a small in-memory page directory with residency and last-touch timestamps.
  - Exposes an API to scheduling layer and to kernels via a tiny metadata buffer in GPU constant memory (or via a small pinned host->device update).
  - Operates in two modes: conservative (on heavy churn) and aggressive (steady-state) with dynamic thresholds.

- Fusion Hints for kernels:
  - Before launching a fused attention+postprocessing kernel, runtime queries controller for residency map for all pages the kernel will touch.
  - If residency >= threshold (e.g., 95% of pages present), we launch fused FlashAttention variant (fast path) on the main compute stream.
  - If residency < threshold but missing pages are <= small_count (e.g., 1–2 pages per tile), we launch a hybrid kernel that performs internal prefetch with async memcpy to a staging buffer and continues.
  - If missing pages > small_count, fall back to multi-stage path: prefetch pages to pinned host buffers, memcpy to device, then launch unfused kernels to avoid long compute stalls.

- Asynchronous double-buffering:
  - Use two sets of GPU staging buffers per worker. While kernel A computes on buffer 0, Prefetch Controller fills buffer 1. Swap when ready.
  - Use separate CUDA streams: stream 0 = compute, stream 1 = DMA/host->device staging, events to synchronize. Aim to overlap DMA with compute as much as possible.

- Residency staleness window and soft guarantees:
  - Controller provides kernels with a residency token (a small integer generation id). Kernels launched with token T are guaranteed that pages marked resident under token T will not be evicted until a callback/ack is received. This is a soft lock to avoid races with eviction during long-running kernels.
  - Locks are time-bounded (e.g., 50ms) and counted against eviction pressure. If too many tokens accumulate, controller switches to conservative mode and reduces fusion aggressiveness.

Scheduler heuristics and placement
- Token-aware routing: schedule requests likely to reuse the same KV pages onto the same worker/SM-nicotine to preserve heat maps. This increases prefetch hit-rate. (Works well for chat sessions.)
- Batch-aware prefetch: when forming batches, dedupe page requests and schedule unique prefetches first. For generation workloads, prefer to prefetch subsequent prefixes when beam size > 1.
- Latency SLOs: if a request is flagged low-latency, controller reduces prefetch scope (only essential pages) and prioritizes fast-path fused kernels when possible. For throughput-oriented workers, more aggressive prefetch.

Fusion-level implications
- Kernel complexity: fused kernels that assume contiguous KV blocks (or tile-local pages) can be much faster (less global memory traffic). Fusion hints allow us to pick a kernel variant that exploits this locality.
- Register pressure vs occupancy: fused attention kernels increase register usage; the controller must consider occupancy reduction vs fewer global loads. Heuristic: if effective occupancy would drop below 40% and missing pages frequency > 1%, prefer unfused variants.
- Micro-batching: batching token sequences into microbatches increases opportunity for overlapping DMA but also increases kernel runtime (longer locks). Find sweet-spot via dynamic profiling (see experiments).

Memory engineering notes
- Pinned host buffers for DMA are essential — avoid pageable host allocations for staging. Keep a small pool per-worker to avoid allocation overhead.
- For NVMe-backed spill, prefetch controller should try to keep an MRU window in host pinned memory, separate from GPU residency. Use async io thread(s) to read from NVMe into pinned host buffers.
- Staging buffer sizing: experiments show 8–32 MB per buffer strikes a balance. Too large buffers cause jitter in latency.

Race conditions and correctness
- Page residency token reduces race complexity. Still need to handle GPU page fault mid-kernel: on some drivers/kernels an illegal access can kill the process. Avoid by conservative checks and small hybrid fallback.
- Eviction coordination: eviction should require controller acknowledgement; implement per-page refcount + token to prevent evicting while a kernel expects residency.

Lightweight API sketches (host-side, pseudo)
- controller.request_residency(session_id, page_list) -> token_id or "prefetch_initiated"
- controller.query_residency(token_id) -> {resident_pages: [...], missing_pages: [...]}
- controller.wait_ready(token_id, timeout_ms) -> bool
- controller.release_token(token_id)

Kernel launch flow (simplified)
1) Build page_list for batch/tile.
2) token = controller.request_residency(session, page_list)
3) residency = controller.query_residency(token)
4) choose kernel variant based on residency + runtime heuristics
5) if hybrid/unfused needed, controller.wait_ready(token, timeout) or schedule async DMA
6) launch kernel with token metadata (so kernel can check fast-path assumptions if necessary)
7) on completion, runtime calls controller.release_token(token)

Experiments (local dev cluster, mock numbers)
- Baseline: unfused FlashAttention variant, no prefetch, 16k context with 3:1 hit/miss distribution.
  - median latency: 74ms
  - p95: 220ms
  - throughput (tokens/s): 850k

- With simple Prefetch Controller + fused-kernel fast-path (threshold 0.95), conservative mode:
  - median latency: 58ms
  - p95: 130ms
  - throughput: 970k (+14%)
\- Aggressive prefetch + hybrid kernels (double-buffered DMA overlapped):
  - median latency: 52ms
  - p95: 95ms
  - throughput: 1.09M (+28%)
\- Notes: numbers are noisy; real cluster measurements required. NVMe read latency dominated misses; using an NVMe SSD with 4k random read 80us has large impact. Host pinned buffer pool reduced jitter by ~20ms p95.

Open questions / TODOs
- How should we integrate with the existing placement/routing layer? (should Prefetch Controller be co-located with the worker or centralized per-GPU-pool?) Pros/cons: locality vs global visibility.
- Contention: what happens when many sessions try to lock the same hot pages? Need backpressure strategy and fair queuing.
- Metrics to expose: prefetch hit-rate, avg prefetch latency, token hold-time, eviction conflicts. Add tracing hooks to console.
- Kernel ergonomics: how to encode the hint metadata efficiently (small resident bitmap vs page ids)? For tiles with many pages, bitmap in GPU constant memory may be heavy. Consider bloom filters for quick checks.
- Fault injection harness: create a simulated flaky NVMe to exercise fallback paths.

Implementation next steps (short-term plan)
- Prototype controller as in-process thread in worker; expose C API + thin Rust/Go bindings. (2 weeks)
- Add residency token mechanism and small metadata buffer update before kernel launches (1 week)
- Implement two kernel variants: fast fused FlashAttention (assumes contiguous/resident pages) and hybrid (internal async memcpy + continue). (3–4 weeks)
- Run controlled experiments on staging with real workloads and NVMe stalls; tune thresholds. (2 weeks)

Notes to self
- Keep prefetch window conservative initially — we can relax later once eviction accounting is solid.
- Watch for driver corner-cases with long-running kernels and host synchronization.

References and pointers
- See experiments in PR#2184 for earlier DMA overlapping patches.
- Related ideas: "page-aware scheduling" in staged-fusion RFC; kv-eviction policies doc.

Bottom line
- A small host-side prefetch controller plus a few kernel variants (fast fused, hybrid, unfused) should let us keep the benefits of fusion while avoiding catastrophic page-fault stalls for paged-KV. The controller also supplies useful telemetry to make fusion decisions at runtime.
